oil.summary: Crude posted a modest recovery Thursday — WTI +1.61% to $71.47, Brent +1.71% to $75.00 — but the one-month picture remains brutal, with both benchmarks down roughly 24% since late May. The day's bounce reflects a stabilisation rather than a reversal: Hormuz flows have resumed and Washington has temporarily lifted Iran oil sanctions, flooding the market with supply expectations that had already been priced in aggressively to the downside. ADNOC trimmed its Murban July OSP to $101.48 from $104.44, confirming easing Gulf premiums. Asian buying interest, which had driven spot markets for three weeks, is now fading. Russia's domestic fuel crunch — 17 regions with mandatory sales restrictions following Ukrainian strikes on refineries — adds a geopolitical wildcard, though Moscow is reportedly using the post-Hormuz chaos to deepen crude ties with Indonesia. Gasoline and heating oil barely moved, suggesting the crude bounce is tentative.
drivers: Hormuz reopening and temporary US suspension of Iran oil sanctions cap the upside, keeping WTI pinned near $71 despite today's bounce
Asian spot crude buying running out of steam after a three-week spree, removing a key demand-side support
Ukrainian strikes deepening Russia's domestic fuel crunch, but Moscow pivoting commercially toward Southeast Asia as a partial offset

gas.summary: Henry Hub and TTF are diverging sharply. Henry Hub gained 1.58% on the day to $3.272/MMBtu, extending a strong one-month rally of +13.06%, while TTF slid 2.71% to €40.876/MWh and is off 16% over the past month. The US demand side is the dominant Henry Hub driver: the Tennessee Valley Authority's preliminary 2026 integrated resource plan confirms AI-driven load growth is already outpacing reserve capacity, pointing to sustained gas-fired power demand. SpaceX's plan to break ground next month on an eight-mile gas pipeline to fuel its operations adds a novel but real demand signal. On the supply side, Ukraine struck a major Russian natural gas plant in its latest long-range attack, compounding the refinery damage that has left 17 Russian regions rationing fuel. TTF weakness likely reflects the broader Hormuz-easing narrative reducing European energy risk premiums.
drivers: AI and data-centre load growth driving US gas demand expectations higher, underpinning Henry Hub's +13% one-month rally
Ukrainian long-range strike on a major Russian natural gas plant adds supply disruption risk on the European side
TTF retreating as Hormuz normalisation deflates the geopolitical risk premium that had supported European gas prices

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs were nearly flat at $76.36 (-0.12% on the day), holding a modest +2.65% one-month gain even as TTF — the key marginal cost input for gas-fired power — fell 2.71% on the day and 16% over the month. The decoupling suggests carbon has its own floor from policy and compliance demand. The headline story for the power sector today is structural: Rystad Energy projects the AI data-centre boom could drive the fuel cell market to $30 billion by 2030 as developers bypass congested grids for on-site generation. The DOE separately says geothermal could power 65 million US homes by 2050. On the geopolitical front, the UK vetoed a Treasury plan to expand North Sea oil and gas drilling for defence funding, while a broad North Sea clean-energy coalition — eight European nations — signals continued offshore power investment. Lithium carbonate futures in China fell roughly 10% over two sessions to a ten-week low, a negative signal for battery storage economics.
drivers: AI data-centre power demand accelerating adoption of on-site fuel cells and straining grid capacity, per Rystad Energy analysis
Lithium carbonate prices dropping ~10% in two sessions to a ten-week low, pressuring battery storage project economics
UK Energy Secretary blocking North Sea drilling expansion for defence funding, keeping UK carbon-reduction policy intact despite fiscal pressure
